title: Voltmeter
short_intro: A voltmeter is a high-resistance measuring instrument used to determine the potential difference between two points in an electrical circuit. It is always connected in parallel across the components whose potential drop is to be measured to minimize current diversion.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Conversion of a galvanometer into a voltmeter by connecting a high series resistance, calculation of multiplier resistance, and basic circuit connection rules.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Loading effect of voltmeters, finite resistance limitations, multi-range voltmeter design, sensitivity expressed in ohms per volt, and calibration using potentiometer arrangements.

prerequisites: Ohm's Law and circuit potential distribution
Moving coil galvanometer principles and torque equation

concept_notes.heading: Basic Principle of Conversion
bullets: A moving coil galvanometer cannot be directly connected across a high potential difference due to its low coil resistance and small full-scale deflection current.
To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a very high resistance (multiplier, R) is connected in series with the galvanometer coil.
The high series resistance limits the total current flowing through the device, protecting the delicate coil from thermal damage while scaling the voltage range.

concept_notes.heading: Ideal vs. Practical Voltmeter
bullets: An ideal voltmeter possesses infinite internal resistance so that it draws zero current from the circuit under test and does not disturb the operating voltages.
A practical voltmeter has a very high, but finite, internal resistance which draws a minute fraction of circuit current, causing a slight loading effect.
Higher resistance per volt (sensitivity) characterizes a better quality voltmeter with minimal circuit disturbance.

concept_notes.heading: Voltmeter Sensitivity
bullets: Voltmeter sensitivity (S) is defined as the reciprocal of the full-scale deflection current (I_g).
It is expressed in ohms per volt (Ω/V), signifying how much resistance the voltmeter introduces per volt of its full-scale rating.
Sensitivity helps determine the loading error when measuring voltages across high-impedance circuit nodes.

concept_notes.heading: Multi-range Voltmeter Design
bullets: A multi-range voltmeter incorporates multiple series resistors connected via a selector switch to provide different voltage measurement scales.
Resistors are calculated individually for each desired voltage range using the galvanometer constant parameters.
Care must be taken to ensure that switching between ranges maintains continuous circuit protection without open-circuiting the coil.

derivations.title: Derivation of Series Resistance (Multiplier) for Voltmeter Conversion
derivations.conditions: Galvanometer of resistance G with full-scale deflection current I_g to be converted to measure a maximum potential difference V.
steps: Let the total resistance of the voltmeter be R_v = G + R, where R is the series resistance to be added.
According to Ohm's law, the maximum voltage V that can be measured corresponds to the full-scale deflection current I_g passing through the total resistance R_v.
Write the equation: V = I_g (G + R).
Rearrange the equation to solve for the required series resistance R: R = (V / I_g) - G.

derivations.title: Derivation of Voltmeter Sensitivity and Range Extension
derivations.conditions: Extending an existing voltmeter range or defining sensitivity S in terms of full-scale current I_g.
steps: Substitute I_g = \frac{1}{S} into the multiplier formula: R = V \cdot S - G.
If a multiplier n is defined as the factor by which the voltage range is increased (n = V / V_g), then V = n I_g G.
Substitute V into the resistance formula to obtain R = G(n - 1).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Calibration of Voltmeter using Potentiometer
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A circuit diagram showing a DC potentiometer wire connected in series with a driver cell and rheostat, a standard cell for standardization, and the test voltmeter connected across a variable potential divider tap along with a standard potentiometer null detector.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Compares the reading indicated by the voltmeter against the exact electromotive force/potential difference measured accurately by the potentiometer without drawing current at null point.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in practical physics viva and numerical problems regarding systematic error correction in voltmeters.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Voltmeter Loading Error Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of measured voltage ratio (V_m / V_t) on the y-axis against the ratio of source resistance to voltmeter resistance (R_{th} / R_v) on the x-axis, showing a hyperbolic decay from 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that as the internal resistance of the voltmeter becomes comparable to the source resistance, the measured voltage drops significantly below the true open-circuit voltage.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual PGT multiple-choice questions on measurement accuracy and finite resistance effects.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Linear Calibration Curve of a Voltmeter
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight-line graph plotting Voltmeter Scale Reading (y-axis) versus Potentiometer True Voltage (x-axis) passing through the origin with a slope equal to unity for an ideal instrument.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Any deviation from the straight-line slope indicates calibration errors, zero errors, or non-linearity in the spring restoring torque of the galvanometer.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate experimental observation tables and graphical error analysis questions.

solved_numericals.question: A galvanometer has a resistance of 50 Ω and gives a full-scale deflection for a current of 2 mA. Calculate the value of the series resistance required to convert it into a voltmeter of range 0 to 10 V.
solution_steps: Identify given values: G = 50 \Omega, I_g = 2 \text{ mA} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}, V = 10 \text{ V}.
Apply the formula for series resistance: R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G.

solved_numericals.question: A voltmeter with a resistance of 10 kΩ is used to measure the potential difference across a 20 kΩ resistor connected in series with a 50 kΩ resistor across a 140 V DC supply. Find the percentage error in the voltage reading caused by the loading effect of the voltmeter.
solution_steps: Calculate the true potential difference across the 20 kΩ resistor without the voltmeter: V_{true} = 140 \times \frac{20}{20 + 50} = 140 \times \frac{2}{7} = 40 \text{ V}.

When the voltmeter of R_v = 10 \text{ k}\Omega is connected in parallel with the 20 kΩ resistor, calculate the equivalent parallel resistance R_p: R_p = \frac{20 \times 10}{20 + 10} = \frac{200}{30} = 6.67 \text{ k}\Omega.
Calculate the total circuit resistance with the voltmeter connected: R_{total} = R_p + 50 = 6.67 + 50 = 56.67 \text{ k}\Omega.
Calculate the total current drawn from the 140 V supply: I = \frac{140}{56.67} \text{ mA}.
Calculate the measured voltage V_{measured} across the parallel combination: V_{measured} = I \times R_p = \frac{140}{56.67} \times 6.67 = 16.48 \text{ V}.
Alternatively, using voltage divider with R_p and 50 k\Omega: V_{measured} = 140 \times \frac{6.67}{6.67 + 50} = 140 \times \frac{6.67}{56.67} = 16.48 \text{ V}.
solved_numericals.answer: -58.8% (voltmeter reads 16.48 V instead of true 40 V due to severe loading)

solved_numericals.question: A moving coil galvanometer has a resistance of 30 Ω and shows full scale deflection for 50 mA. How can it be converted into a multi-range voltmeter to measure 0-10 V, 0-50 V, and 0-100 V using a single galvanometer?
solution_steps: Given parameters: G = 30 \Omega, I_g = 50 \text{ mA} = 0.05 \text{ A}.
For range V_2 = 50 \text{ V}: Total resistance required in series R_{total2} = \frac{50}{0.05} = 1000 \Omega. The additional series resistor between 10V and 50V taps is R_2 = 1000 - 200 = 800 \Omega.
For range V_3 = 100 \text{ V}: Total resistance required R_{total3} = \frac{100}{0.05} = 2000 \Omega. The additional series resistor between 50V and 100V taps is R_3 = 2000 - 1000 = 1000 \Omega.
solved_numericals.answer: Series resistors of 170 \Omega, 800 \Omega, and 1000 \Omega connected in a step-ladder arrangement.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Galvanometer deflection is strictly linear with current, which holds only within elastic limits of the control hairsprings.
Limitation: Real voltmeters draw non-zero current, altering high-impedance circuit nodes (loading effect).
Limitation: Standard moving coil DC voltmeters cannot directly measure alternating voltages without rectification.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An ideal voltmeter has zero resistance so that it does not impede current flow.
common_misconceptions.correct: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
common_misconceptions.why: Infinite resistance ensures that no current is diverted from the main circuit through the voltmeter branch.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Connecting a voltmeter in series with a circuit component measures the voltage across it.
common_misconceptions.correct: A voltmeter must always be connected in parallel across the component.
common_misconceptions.why: Parallel connection ensures the same potential difference exists across both the component and the voltmeter terminals.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A voltmeter's range can be increased by connecting a low shunt resistance in parallel.
common_misconceptions.correct: A high resistance must be connected in series.
common_misconceptions.why: Shunt resistance is used for ammeters to divert current, whereas voltmeters require high series resistance to drop excess voltage.

quick_revision: Required Series Resistance: R = (V / I_g) - G.
Voltmeter Sensitivity S = 1 / I_g (measured in Ω/V).
Always connected in parallel across circuit elements.
